kurz: Which country taxes foreign dividends first, how much of that tax the US credits, what applies to accounts and funds abroad, and when giving up US status triggers an exit tax.

bloecke.md:
In a US brokerage account that holds US stocks, the tax mechanics are simple. The broker reports dividends and sales on Form 1099, and you carry the figures over to your return. As soon as a portfolio has a foreign connection, this breaks down at three points. First, the country where the income originates usually taxes it first, before the US does. Second, a broker or fund outside the US sends no Form 1099, and foreign funds fall under a punitive set of US rules. Third, the US taxes its citizens on their worldwide income wherever they live. Moving abroad therefore does not end US tax obligations, and giving up citizenship or a long-held green card can itself trigger tax on gains that were never realized.

The three cases are not related in substance, but all of them are underestimated.

## Foreign withholding and the foreign tax credit

If a Swiss company pays a dividend to a US investor, Switzerland withholds 35% by law. The income tax treaty between the US and Switzerland limits Switzerland's claim on portfolio dividends to 15%, but the full 35% is generally withheld at source, and the excess has to be reclaimed from the Swiss authorities. Many other treaty countries also stop at 15%; some, such as the United Kingdom, levy no withholding tax on dividends at all.

So that the same income is not taxed in full twice, the US allows a **foreign tax credit** (26 U.S.C. § 901). It reduces your US income tax dollar for dollar. Two limits apply. Only the tax you actually owe the foreign country counts; an amount you could get back under a treaty is not a creditable tax, even if you never file the refund claim. And under § 904, the credit cannot exceed the US tax that falls on your foreign-source income. Your broker shows the foreign tax paid in box 7 of Form 1099-DIV.

bloecke.formel: Credit = min(Foreign tax owed under the treaty, US tax × Foreign-source taxable income ÷ Worldwide taxable income)
bloecke.erklaerung: The second term is the § 904 limitation. Form 1116 computes it separately by category of income, with portfolio dividends and interest in the passive category, and adjusts it for qualified dividends taxed at the lower rates. Foreign tax above the limit can be carried back one year and forward ten years.

bloecke.md:
Instead of the credit, you can deduct foreign taxes as an itemized deduction on Schedule A. For $150 of Dutch tax, the deduction saves $33 at a 22% marginal rate, and only if you itemize at all. Most households do not, because the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly for 2026) exceeds their itemized deductions. The credit saves the full $150. You have to choose one method for all foreign taxes of the year, and the credit wins in almost every case.

For small amounts there is a simplification. If all your foreign taxes come from portfolio income reported on payee statements such as Form 1099-DIV and total no more than $300 ($600 married filing jointly), you can claim the credit directly on Schedule 3 without Form 1116. The § 904 limitation then does not apply, but neither does the carryover of unused amounts.

bloecke.titel: Swiss dividend of $1,000 gross without reclaim
bloecke.unter: The $200 above the treaty rate is not a creditable tax and does not reduce US tax on any return.

bloecke.md:
Inside a traditional IRA, a Roth IRA or a 401(k), dividends are not taxed currently, so there is no US tax against which a foreign tax could be credited. Foreign withholding on dividends paid into these accounts is lost for good. The same applies to a US fund that passes foreign taxes through to its shareholders: held in a retirement account, the pass-through has no use.

A comparable loss can occur in a taxable account in a year in which you owe no federal income tax at all, because a nonrefundable credit has nothing to reduce. With Form 1116, the unused amount can at least be carried back one year and forward ten years. For these reasons, some investors hold international stock funds in taxable accounts and US stocks or bonds in retirement accounts. The effect is real, but usually small compared with the other factors of asset location.

## Foreign taxes inside funds

With funds and ETFs, foreign withholding tax is paid by the fund, not by you. A US mutual fund or ETF that holds more than 50% of its assets in foreign stock at the end of its tax year can elect to pass the foreign taxes through to its shareholders (26 U.S.C. § 853). You then report your share as additional dividend income and claim it as a credit; it appears in box 7 of Form 1099-DIV. A broad international or emerging markets index fund typically qualifies. A global fund that is mostly invested in US stocks usually does not, and the foreign tax then simply reduces the fund's income without any credit.

The fund's domicile matters even more. A fund domiciled outside the US, for example an Irish or Luxembourg UCITS ETF, is a **passive foreign investment company (PFIC)** for a US investor. The withholding tax it pays cannot be credited by you, and without an election the PFIC rules tax gains and large distributions at the highest ordinary rates of earlier years plus an interest charge. For most European funds, the only practical election is annual mark-to-market taxation as ordinary income. Each fund generally requires its own Form 8621 every year. For US investors, US-domiciled funds are therefore the rule, and the UCITS ETFs common in Europe are not an alternative.

bloecke.formel: Leakage in percentage points p.a. ≈ Foreign share × Dividend yield × Withholding tax rate
bloecke.erklaerung: In a taxable account, the pass-through credit offsets most of this leakage. It remains a cost where the credit cannot be used, that is in retirement accounts and in funds that do not qualify for the pass-through. The formula gives an order of magnitude, not an exact figure.
bloecke.beispiel: Illustrative assumptions: for an international stock fund with a foreign share of 100%, a dividend yield of 3% and an average withholding rate of 10%, the result is 1.0 × 3% × 10% = 0.3 percentage points a year.

bloecke.titel: Effect of 0.3 percentage points over 30 years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a lump-sum investment of $100,000 and a gross return of 6.5% a year, without further costs and taxes. The lower line corresponds to an international fund in an IRA, where the foreign tax cannot be credited.

bloecke.md: A US broker asks you for Form W-9, on which you certify that you are a US person and give your Social Security number or other taxpayer identification number. Form W-8BEN is the counterpart for foreign persons: with it, a non-US investor claims the treaty rate on US dividends, for example 15% instead of 30%. If you moved to the US and became a tax resident, a W-8BEN you once gave a broker no longer applies and must be replaced by a W-9. Without a valid W-9, the broker must apply backup withholding of 24% to dividends and sale proceeds (26 U.S.C. § 3406). Backup withholding is credited on your return, but it ties up money for months.

## Accounts and brokers abroad

A broker outside the US, for example a German bank account kept after moving, does not issue Form 1099. This does not save any tax; it only shifts the work and the risk to you. US citizens and residents must report worldwide income, including interest, dividends and gains in foreign accounts, in dollars. Leaving them out makes the return incorrect, and doing so willfully is tax evasion (26 U.S.C. § 7201). The IRS learns about such accounts anyway: under FATCA, foreign financial institutions report accounts held by US persons.

In addition, two information reports apply regardless of the income. The **FBAR** (FinCEN Form 114) is required if the combined maximum value of all your foreign financial accounts exceeded $10,000 at any time during the year. It is filed electronically with FinCEN, not with the tax return, and is due April 15 with an automatic extension to October 15. **Form 8938** is attached to the tax return. For taxpayers living in the US, it is required above $50,000 at year-end or $75,000 at any time during the year (single), and above $100,000 or $150,000 for married couples filing jointly. Penalties for missing either report can far exceed the tax at stake. In Bittner v. United States (2023), the Supreme Court held that the non-willful FBAR penalty applies per report, not per account, which limits the risk but does not remove it.

Many foreign banks and brokers no longer accept US persons as customers or restrict them to cash accounts, partly because of these reporting duties and partly because foreign funds would be PFICs for them.

schritte.text: Record interest, dividends, short-term and long-term gains separately for each account. Part III of Schedule B asks whether you had a foreign account, and it has to be answered.

Translate the cost of each purchase at the exchange rate on the purchase date and the proceeds at the rate on the sale date, not at an annual average. The currency effect therefore becomes part of the taxable gain.

In partial sales, the shares bought first count as sold first unless you specifically identified other lots at the time of sale. A foreign broker's statement may follow another method, which is not decisive for US purposes.
Foreign funds and ETFs generally require Form 8621. Check this before buying, because the consequences can hardly be repaired afterwards.
For the credit, keep the dividend statements that show the foreign tax actually withheld. File the FBAR and, where the thresholds are met, Form 8938.

bloecke.md:
The federal return is due April 15 of the following year. Form 4868 extends the filing deadline to October 15, but not the payment deadline. US citizens living abroad get an automatic two-month extension to June 15. Because nobody withholds tax on income in a foreign account, the tax is due through quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) on April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15. You avoid the underpayment penalty if withholding and estimated payments cover at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax, or 110% if last year's adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000. It makes sense to put the estimated tax into a separate account as soon as the income is received.

The 0% bracket for long-term gains and qualified dividends is not lost in this case. It is applied on the return, regardless of where the account is held.

## Expatriation tax

US citizens who move abroad remain subject to US tax on their worldwide income. The US is one of very few countries that tax on the basis of citizenship. Only renouncing citizenship, or giving up a green card held in at least eight of the last fifteen years, ends this, and that step can itself trigger tax. Under 26 U.S.C. § 877A, a **covered expatriate** is treated as having sold all assets at fair market value on the day before expatriation. The tax falls due although no money flows.

You are a covered expatriate if one of three tests applies: a net worth of $2 million or more, an average annual net income tax over the previous five years above an inflation-adjusted threshold ($206,000 for 2025), or failure to certify on Form 8854 that you met your US tax obligations for the previous five years. The deemed gain is reduced by an inflation-adjusted exclusion amount ($890,000 for 2025). An IRA is treated as distributed in full on the day before expatriation. The $2 million threshold is not indexed for inflation, so a portfolio built up over decades can exceed it even for ordinary savers. Advice is therefore necessary before giving up US status; a rule of thumb is not sufficient.

Moving between states raises a smaller version of the same question. Each state taxes its residents under its own rules, and some examine the year of a move closely, especially when a large gain is realized shortly after leaving.

Extra costs from foreign investments only arise from foreign tax that cannot be credited. This means withholding above the treaty rate, withholding in retirement accounts or in years without US income tax, and withholding inside funds that cannot pass it through. The first can be reclaimed, the second can be reduced through the choice of account, and the third only through the choice of fund.

The refund is handled by the tax authority of the source country, not by the IRS. There is usually a separate form, a separate deadline and a certificate of US residency, which the IRS issues as Form 6166 on application with Form 8802, for a user fee. Switzerland forfeits the claim three years after the end of the calendar year in which the dividend fell due (Article 32 of the Swiss Withholding Tax Act). For ADRs, depositary banks sometimes arrange relief at source or a refund, usually for a fee.

With an excess of 20 percentage points, every $1,000 of dividends brings a refund of $200. With $300 of Swiss dividends a year, the forms therefore yield $60, less the fee for the residency certificate. The effort only becomes worthwhile for significant amounts. Alternatively, several years can be collected and combined in one application within the deadline.

It is simpler to cover countries with a high excess through a US fund rather than through individual shares. Within the fund, the reclaim is handled institutionally.

mitnehmen: The US credits foreign tax only up to the treaty rate and only up to the US tax on the foreign income (§ 904); anything withheld beyond the treaty rate can only be reclaimed in the source country.
The credit reduces US tax dollar for dollar and beats the itemized deduction in almost every case; up to $300 of foreign tax ($600 jointly) can be claimed without Form 1116.
In IRAs, Roth IRAs and 401(k)s, foreign withholding cannot be credited and is lost; US international funds pass foreign taxes through to you, but this only helps in a taxable account.
Foreign funds are PFICs for US investors, and foreign accounts bring FBAR and Form 8938 duties; a foreign broker saves no tax, it only shifts the work to you.
Moving abroad does not end US taxation for citizens; giving up citizenship or a long-held green card can trigger a deemed sale of all assets under § 877A.

begriffe.text: Credit under 26 U.S.C. § 901 that reduces US income tax by foreign income tax paid, limited to the treaty rate and, under § 904, to the US tax on foreign-source income. Unused amounts can be carried back one year and forward ten years.

Form on which individuals compute the foreign tax credit and the § 904 limitation by category of income. It is not needed if all foreign taxes come from portfolio income reported on payee statements and total no more than $300, or $600 on a joint return.

Foreign corporation whose income is mainly passive or whose assets mainly produce passive income, which covers almost all funds and ETFs domiciled outside the US. Without an election, gains and large distributions are taxed at the highest ordinary rates plus an interest charge; reporting is on Form 8621.

Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FinCEN Form 114), required for US persons whose foreign financial accounts together exceeded $10,000 at any time during the year. It is filed with FinCEN, separately from the tax return.

US citizen or long-term green card holder who gives up that status and meets the net worth test ($2 million) or the tax liability test, or cannot certify five years of tax compliance. Under § 877A, all assets are treated as sold on the day before expatriation.
